title: AetherGrid p95 concurrency & tokenflow assessment
meeting_header: Date: 2027-03-09 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Rahul (CTO), Elena (Lead ML), Marco (Infra)
summary: Introductory discovery to map AetherGrid's p95 latency targets and token/sec burst profile for their real-time summarization product. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, streaming behavior, KV cache usage, and initial benchmark plan. Agreed to a short pilot + security package and a benchmark spreadsheet to capture token/sec distributions.
topics: steady-state and burst concurrency (10, 50, 200 concurrent streams)
streaming token/sec patterns and token bursts per session
hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) decision criteria
benchmarking plan: token/sec, end-to-end p95, coldstart vs warm
security requirements: SOC 2, SAML SSO, KMS/HSM, data residency
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm samira from Redwood Inference. quick roll call?
[00:08] Rahul: rahul here, CTO at aethergrid. thanks Samira.
[00:12] Elena: elena, lead ml engineer, hi.
[00:15] Marco: marco, infra, hi.
[00:18] Liam: liam, solution eng on the redwood side, hi all.
[00:22] Samira: great, goal for today is to understand your p95 targets and tokenflow so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private and a pilot. feel free to interrupt.
[00:34] Rahul: sure. high level - our core product does realtime meeting summarization. typical session is a user streaming audio -> transcripts -> long-form context and we stream back the summary tokens. we want p95 latency under 200ms ideally for short responses, but for longer summaries p95 at 500ms is acceptable. also bursts happen when multiple participants request clarifications; so concurrency spikes to what feels like 150-200 streams for short 2-3s replies.
[00:58] Elena: to add, average session generates about 200-600 tokens per summary, but we have many small messages of 10-60 tokens for clarifications. tokenburst distribution is heavy tail.
[01:12] Liam: ok got it. when you say p95 200ms is that end-to-end (audio->text->summary) or token-streaming latency on the model side?
[01:22] Rahul: model-only, once transcript is ready and call to the inference endpoint begins. we handle ASR separately. so we care about token generation latency and time-to-first-token too.
[01:31] Samira: good clarification. so two main metrics: time-to-first-token (TTFT) and p95 for complete response and token throughput (tokens/sec). also need to account for concurrency and warm vs cold KV cache state.
[01:45] Elena: question - we currently run a local quantized model for experiments. we see good per-token speed but memory and scaling is hard. considering redwood to move to hosted or dedicated. what's the typical latency delta?
[01:58] Liam: it depends. hosted shared infra has scheduling latency and multi-tenant noise but we optimize for streaming. for p95 at 200ms with short outputs (10-50 tokens) we'd probably recommend dedicated or higher-tier hosted with reserved cpus/gpus. dedicated gives predictable throughput - you control pool sizing and we can reserve GPU pools.
[02:17] Marco: do you support VPC/private deployments for compliance? we have EU data residency and some controls needed.
[02:23] Samira: yes, we have Redwood Private with customer-managed VPCs and on-prem options. we can integrate with your KMS and activate audit logs. SOC2 and SAML SSO integration are supported. we'll attach security pack.
[02:33] Rahul: good. back to benchmarking — can you walk us through what you need to reproduce our p95 numbers?
[02:39] Liam: typically we ask for representative prompt sets, token length distribution, concurrency profile (sessions per minute, peak bursts), and a clear p95 definition (end-to-end model response or per-token). we'll run token/sec microbenchmarks and end-to-end latency benchmarks under load. for streaming, we'll measure time-to-first-token, steady-state token/sec, and p95 for completion.
[03:02] Elena: how do KV cache and prefix caching affect streaming? some of our workloads reuse context across turns.
[03:08] Liam: prefix/KV caching can dramatically reduce p95 for repeated prefixes. if you have reuse we can keep KV warm; the runtime supports automatic KV cache management and we can tune eviction policies. warm cache vs cold can easily be 2-3x difference on p95 in heavy workloads.
[03:23] Rahul: can we get an example recommendation? say target p95 200ms, average output 30 tokens, 150 concurrent streams. what would you propose?
[03:31] Liam: rough rule of thumb - for modern Llama-style medium models on A100-class GPUs, with continuous batching & streaming optimizations, you might need 3-4 GPUs dedicated to sustain 150 concurrent short streaming sessions at ~30 tokens with p95 near 200ms. exact number depends on model config, sequence length, quantization, and kernel optimizations. for hosted we could map to a higher-tier plan with guaranteed concurrency slices.
[03:55] Elena: we use a 16k context model at times, that pushes memory. how does that change things?
[04:01] Liam: longer context increases memory footprint and KV cache pressure; per-token cost increases slightly due to KV reads. for 16k you might need larger GPU memory or more sharding. Dedicated or private with GPU variants that support 80GB memory or multi-GPU sharding would be a safer choice.
[04:17] Marco: what about cold starts and scale-to-zero? we have infrequent but large bursts from scheduled events. we can't afford 30s cold starts.
[04:26] Samira: we support reserved capacity with burst pools; autoscaling policies can keep a minimum warm pool to meet p95 SLOs. scale-to-zero is available but not for real-time SLOs; recommend a warm buffer for scheduled events.
[04:39] Rahul: any options for reducing cost while keeping p95? quantization? batching?
[04:44] Liam: yes - quantization (int8 or newer quant profiles) reduces memory and can speed up per-token inference slightly, but be careful with quality regressions. intelligent batching and prefix caching are the biggest levers — batching improves throughput but can add head-of-line latency if not continuously streamed; our runtime does continuous batching tuned for streaming. Also you can configure a fallthrough policy to a cheaper model variant for non-critical paths.
[05:06] Elena: how accurate is quantization at preserving summary quality? we have strict quality thresholds.
[05:11] Liam: depends on model and quant strategy; we run eval sets tied to your prompt set and will report ROUGE/BERTScore deltas vs baseline. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles and alert on regressions.
[05:24] Marco: latency jitter is a concern - network variability in hosted setups. how do you measure and guarantee p95?
[05:30] Samira: p95 SLOs for hosted are driven by regional routing and our observability. we provide token-level latency breakdowns in Console so you can see queueing vs model vs network. Dedicated and Private reduce network jitter by placing runtime closer to your infra.
[05:44] Rahul: any competitors you've benchmarked against for low-latency streaming?
[05:48] Liam: we do internal comparisons but i'll share a high-level matrix - some vendors prioritize throughput over per-token latency. we can include a competitive note in the benchmark results.
[05:58] Elena: ok practical next steps? we want to run a benchmark that matches our burst profile and see p95 numbers.
[06:05] Liam: propose this: you share a token distribution spreadsheet, example prompts, and a simulated concurrency curve (CSV). Redwood will run two bench types: micro token/sec to characterize model runtime, and an end-to-end streaming load test matching your concurrency profile including warm/cold cache runs.
[06:21] Samira: we'll also attach our security pack (SOC2, SSO docs, data residency options) and propose a pilot: 2-week pilot with a dedicated pool (2 GPUs to start) to replicate bursts. pricing for dedicated pilot and hosted options will be included.
[06:36] Rahul: timeline? we need numbers for leadership in two weeks.
[06:40] Samira: ok we'll prioritize. we'll aim to deliver initial bench report in 10 business days if we get artifacts by end of week.
[06:48] Marco: what telemetry will you need? logs, traces?
[06:52] Liam: we ask for sample prompt/response pairs and a small client that simulates streaming behavior (we can provide a harness). logs/traces optional; we integrate tracing hooks for better analysis.
[07:04] Elena: any gotchas with VPC/private? latency to our downstream systems matters.
[07:09] Samira: for private, network topology is critical. we'll do a network whiteboard with your infra team during onboarding. encryption in transit + KMS for at-rest keys.
[07:19] Rahul: ok good. if you could include explicit recommendations for sustain 150 concurrent streams p95 200ms and for heavy 16k contexts that'd be great.
[07:26] Liam: absolutely. summary of action items coming up.
[07:30] (crosstalk)
[07:32] Samira: quick recap: 1) AetherGrid shares token distribution and concurrency CSV; 2) Redwood provides benchmark harness + pilot proposal and security pack; 3) schedule follow-up for results in ~10 business days.
[07:48] Rahul: sounds good. thanks all.
[07:52] Elena: thanks.
[07:54] Marco: thanks.
[07:56] Liam: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with next steps and the harness repo link.
[07:59] Samira: end.
